why: This is one of the few places where the Plain leaves Vaticanus. Its short text says the army "went back … for a hundred and twenty days," which makes little sense, and the longer text explains the 120 days as a victory feast. A scribe's eye most likely jumped from the first autos ("he") to the second, dropping the words between. Of the longer text the Plain follows Sinaiticus, without "to Nineveh": a single witness adds it, and it reads like a scribe's explanation of where "back" was.
b: Where the king went back to is not said in Sinaiticus or Vaticanus, but the story implies Nineveh, his city (1:1; 2:21). The feast of 120 days answers the feast of Ahasuerus in Esther 1:4 ("180 days").

p: Sinaiticus lacks "not". Then the line reads "so that he may do as we have said today", a demand on Uzziah.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; the KJV follows this text
readings.orig: ἵνα μὴ ποιήσῃ κατὰ τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τῇ σήμερον
readings.en: so that he may not do according to these words this very day
readings.plain: May he not do to us today what we have described!

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Swete's apparatus
readings.en: so that he may do according to these words this very day
readings.plain: So let him do today as we have said!

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus and Alexandrinus. With "not," God is asked not to bring on them the deaths they have just described (7:27). Without it, the people demand that Uzziah do as they said and surrender today. Sinaiticus's reading is simpler, and may be a correction of a hard line, or the original sense.
